title: History comes home: 1937, 1970 fire engines return to Hanover area - NewsBreak
text: Two pieces of Hanover area fire service history are returning to Hanover for the first time in decades to be preserved for generations to come. The Greater Hanover Area Fire Museum has purchased back two historic fire engines that once served the streets of Hanover, including an engine dating from 1937, and a second engine that dates to 1970, said museum president Gordy Lillich. On Wednesday morning, Aug. 6, 2025, the first of the two engines, a 1937 American LaFrance with the radio designation of 139, arrived back in its hometown. The second engine, a 1970 American LaFrance 900 model pumper, is expected to be brought back to Hanover within the next two weeks. The 1937 American LaFrance 400 Junior pumper served Hanover from 1937 to 1970, Lillich said, and was then sold to a private collector, Lewis Dielman, in Elder, Montana. The pumper had been kept mostly inside of a barn, mostly preserving the original apparatus from any significant damage. Three local businesses, Aero Energy of New Oxford, Ox Industries of Hanover and Bosley Towing of Littlestown, all donated towards bringing the engine back from Montana, assisting with transportation and costs, Lillich said. "Everybody here has been anxiously awaiting it," said Lillich. Among the unique quirks of the 1937 engine, recalled retired Hanover Fire Commissioner Jim Roth who once drove the vehicle, were side-mounted ladders that blocked access to the driver's seat, requiring drivers to enter from the passenger's side. For some in attendance at the arrival of the 1937 engine, the moment was a personal one. Edward Markle, who grew up next door to the Eagle Fire Company that now houses the fire museum, recalls seeing the engine leave for Montana when he was just six-years-old. The most distinct feature that Markle could recall of the engine was a large metal bell on the front of it - which he notes was prominently displayed at his six-year-old eye level. Due to the transportation from Montana, the bell had been temporarily removed to protect it while in transit, but will be added back on. "I haven't seen this truck since it left here 55 years ago," Markle recalled. At the time, his bedroom window was right in line with the fire station's bell tower, making him well aware whenever the engine would get a call. Among those who would respond to those calls for help was Markle's father, John Markle, who rode the 1937 engine Seeing the engine once again within the walls of the Eagle Fire Company made Markle think of his father, he said. "I'm just glad to see it back," said Markle, who added that he was also excited for the return of the 1970 engine, which he remembers being delivered to the firehouse. The 1970 engine served the Hanover area from 1970 to 2000, and was recently retired by the West Fork Fire Department, coincidentally also located in Montana. In addition to the two new engines, the museum's permanent collection already includes three other historic Hanover fire apparatus: a 1961 International fire engine, a 1934 Gramam Dodge Brother Buffalo engine, and a 1882 Silsby Steamer. The Greater Hanover Area Fire Museum is located at 134 East Hanover Street and is open the first, second and third Saturdays of each month from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., as well as from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. every Wednesday. Admission to the museum is free, though donations are accepted. Harrison Jones is the Hanover reporter for the Evening Sun. Reach him at hjones@gannett.com .
